title: La Bohème
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,415th Bohème. The first was on 26 December 1900, with Nellie Melba as Mimì.
Host Matthew Polenzani knows this garret: the tenor has sung La Bohème at the Gran Teatre del Liceu.
Zeffirelli’s garret: a cutaway attic perched on the Paris rooftops, complete with tiles and smoking chimney pots.
Thor Eckert Jr., The Christian Science Monitor, on this production’s Met premiere, 14 Dec 1981
Our Marcello, Lucas Meachem, got his big break in 2006, discovered by Susan Graham at a karaoke bar. In Paris.
Bohème’s premiere, Turin, 1 February 1896, was conducted by a 28-year-old Arturo Toscanini.
Juliana Grigoryan, our Mimì, won first and audience prizes at Operalia 2022. Her Met debut: Liù, in 2024.
Puccini on this opera: “I lived that Bohème”, as a poor student, short of food, clothes and rent.
“Che gelida manina” comes in three paragraphs: tender, then bolder at “Chi son? Sono un poeta”, then the love motif.
Listen for the climactic high C on “speranza”: it’s unwritten, not in Puccini’s score.
Our Rodolfo, Freddie De Tommaso, entered London’s Royal Academy of Music as a baritone, then became a tenor.
As they realize they’re in love, the love motif from “Che gelida manina” returns.
The ending: Mimì’s high C, marked “fading away”, over descending harp harmonics. A major has become C major.
When this Act II set was unveiled in 1981, the audience roared for nearly a minute.
Thor Eckert Jr., The Christian Science Monitor, on this production’s Met premiere, 14 Dec 1981
A stilt walker, a dancing bear, Musetta’s horse-drawn cab: “a Delacroix riot of reds and golds.”
Charles Michener, Newsweek, 28 Dec 1981, on this production’s Met premiere
Conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson made her Met debut in 2022–23. She also founded the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra.
Musetta’s Waltz is aimed at the people in the café as much as at us in the theater.
Heidi Stober began as a pianist and first planned to teach choral music. Then came opera.
The act ends in a parade. At the 1981 premiere it brought some 240 people onto the Met stage.
Thor Eckert Jr., The Christian Science Monitor, on this production’s Met premiere, 14 Dec 1981
Watch the tavern door: a man in black rushes out, opens a black umbrella, and vanishes into the snow.
Charles Michener, Newsweek, 28 Dec 1981, on this production’s Met premiere, calling it a “ghostly bit of stage business”
Two couples, two moods: Mimì and Rodolfo part tenderly while Marcello and Musetta quarrel fiercely.
Check the sky behind the garret: silver-gray in Act I, rosy-peach now in Act IV.
Charles Michener, Newsweek, 28 Dec 1981, on this production’s Met premiere
Zeffirelli turns Colline and Schaunard’s mock duel into a mad scamper along the rooftops.
Charles Michener, Newsweek, 28 Dec 1981, on this production’s Met premiere
Jongmin Park bids farewell to Colline’s coat. He made his Covent Garden debut in this very role, in 2014.
Bohème closed the old Met house in April 1966. Zeffirelli then staged the new house’s very first production.
